CHENNAI: A 45-year-old woman and her 23-year-old daughter were killed in an accident after a private school bus collided with their two-wheeler near Urapakkam on Wednesday morning. The deceased were identified as Devi and Swathi, residents of a Tamil Nadu Urban Habitat Development Board quarters at Keerapakkam near Guduvanchery.
Police said Swathi was riding the two-wheeler with her mother seated pillion. The duo had left their house and were heading towards Urapakkam.
When they were nearing Karanai Padur village, Swathi attempted to overtake a government bus, when a private school bus coming from the opposite direction collided with it. On impact, both were grievously injured, and Devi died on the spot.
Swathi who was rushed to a private hospital in Potheri was declared ‘brought dead’ by the arrival. The Guduvanchery Traffic Investigation Wing sent the bodies for post-mortem to the Tambaram GH.
Police said there were no students inside the school bus at the time of the accident. Only the driver and his assistant were travelling in the vehicle.
The police have registered a case and are questioning the bus driver. It is learnt that Swathi had recently been engaged and was scheduled to get married next month.

A trip to Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh ended in tragedy for two families in Karnataka after four people were killed and three others injured when their Innova crashed into a stone culvert near Doddakari village in Kolar Gold Fields (KGF) on Monday morning.
The police identified the dead as Devendra, 44, his mother-in-law Sharadha Bai, 70, and Devendra’s children, Deeksha, 20, and Vishnu Sai, 12— all residents of Mysuru. The injured victims have been hospitalised.
According to the police, families of two sisters—one based in Bengaluru and the other in Mysuru—set out for Tirumala for darshan around 3 am and were returning home when the accident occurred around 7 am.
The police said the Innova’s driver, Vikas Rao, likely dozed off at the wheel, causing the car to veer off and strike the roadside culvert.
Since the Bengaluru-Chennai Expressway opened to traffic in March 2025, the section between Kolathur near Hoskote and Bethamangala has recorded over a dozen accidents and nearly 25 deaths.
In another incident, three women labourers were killed in Chikkaballapur district after an Omni van and a mini-goods vehicle collided near Kothanur Gate in Shidlaghatta taluk around 2.30 am, according to the police. The women are Roopa, 30, Rathnamma, 45, and Munichinnamma, 40—all residents of Mallikarjunapura
The victims were heading for harvesting flowers near Huzuguru village.
A police officer said, “The women were travelling in the Omni van which was driven by one Ramachandrappa. The van collided with a mini goods vehicle, and they died on the spot. There were about 10 daily-wage labourers. The injured were shifted to a nearby hospital for treatment.”
The police suspect that the driver of either the goods vehicle or the Omni van may have dozed off, leading to the collision. They have registered a case.

CHENNAI: A motor accident claims tribunal in Chennai has ordered a two-wheeler dealer, who allowed a new bike to be used on a public road without even having a temporary registration number, and the bike owner to pay a compensation of 97.18 lakh jointly to the family of a man who was fatally knocked down by the vehicle. 
Judge Dharmaprabhu passed the order awarding Rs 97.18 lakh as compensation to the family of Balamuthu Murugan, an assistant professor at Loyola College, who was killed in a road accident at Gummidipoondi in 2017.
Murugan was riding his motorcycle when a newly purchased two-wheeler, driven rashly and negligently and coming in the opposite direction, collided with his vehicle, resulting in his death.
His wife, children and mother moved the tribunal seeking a compensation of Rs 53 lakh. After examining the evidence, the tribunal enhanced the compensation to Rs 97.18 lakh. It further held that the dealer could not escape liability as the new vehicle had been permitted to ply on a public road without securing even a temporary registration, in violation of the law.
The tribunal directed the vehicle owner and the dealer to jointly deposit the compensation amount within one month.

Abstract
This study presents a comprehensive analysis of road accidents in India by using official government data sets from 53 major cities across 28 states. This research is conducted under a Type-2 picture fuzzy environment with advanced aggregation operators such as the arithmetic mean, geometric mean, hamy mean, Einstein weighted operator, and Aczel-Alsina operator. To enhance decision-making under uncertainty, a novel distance measure is proposed and theoretically validated. Five prominent distance-based multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS, and COPRAS were applied to rank the cities based on 35 critical road accident-related criteria. The results of the model revealed that Chennai consistently secured the top ranking in TOPSIS, COPRAS, and FIR. Amritsar also performed exceptionally, ranking 1st in VIKOR and achieving 3rd in TOPSIS. In contrast, cities such as Kanpur, Lucknow, and Ahmedabad consistently ranked in the bottom quartile, with Kanpur receiving the lowest position (53rd) in TOPSIS and FIR, indicating they are in critical risk zones. Mid-ranked cities such as Hyderabad, Pune, and Rajkot showed variations across methods but maintained stable FIR positions. To validate the robustness of the rankings, a comprehensive sensitivity analysis was conducted by various decision parameter q, confirming the stability of rankings under fluctuating conditions. The proposed framework improved the precision of accident severity and demonstrated adaptability to broader decision-making scenarios involving uncertainty. This study contributes a novel, integrated, and mathematically rigorous methodology for assessing urban safety for policymakers to reduce the road accident risks across Indian cities.

Introduction
Road accidents are one of the leading causes of death and injury globally, posing a serious threat to public health and safety. According to the WHO report approximately 1.3 million people die each year as a result of road traffic crashes1. Millions more suffer non-fatal injuries, often leading to long-term disabilities and emotional trauma. The burden is disproportionately higher in low- and middle-income countries, where 93% of the world’s road fatalities occur despite having only 60% of the vehicles. Road accidents affect individuals, families and also the broader economy system. The economic cost of road traffic accidents is estimated at 3% of a country’s GDP in many nations. Emergency medical services, insurance payouts and productivity loss contribute significantly to these financial burdens. Children, young adults and working-age individuals are most vulnerable loss to the nation’s human capital. In urban areas traffic accidents contribute to congestion, delays and pollution. Globally road accidents are considered as a development issue and also a traffic concern2.
Preventing road accidents aligns with the UNSDG especially goal 3 (good health and well-being) and goal 11 (sustainable cities and communities). Enhanced infrastructure, proper urban planning and vehicle safety standards are key to reducing risks. Strong enforcement of traffic laws including penalties for drunk driving, speeding and mobile phone use has proven effective in many countries3. Public awareness and education campaigns play a crucial role in shaping road behavior. Vehicle maintenance and technological advancements such as ABS, lane-assist systems and collision warnings have improved safety4.
In many parts of the world roads have poor conditions, lack of enforcement and limited awareness. Data collection and research into road accident provides help in formulating effective policies. International cooperation and knowledge exchange strengthen global road safety efforts5. Developing nations are prioritising road safety in policy frameworks and budgets.
Road safety is a responsibility which involving governments, engineers, law enforcement and road users. Reducing accidents helps economic development with social well-being. Safer roads ensure better mobility, access to education and healthcare in both urban and rural areas. Addressing this issue can transform the path of people travel and live.
India has one of the highest rates of road accidents globally which providing continuous analysis and interventions. According to the MoRTH over 1.5 lakh people die in road crashes annually in India6. Road accidents in India have emerged as a critical public safety issue with severe socio-economic and health implications. These accidents lead to tragic loss of life and also result in millions of injuries. Most of these cause a long-term disability and trauma. These accidents cause loss of life and massive economic setbacks with long-term trauma for families. Most fatalities occur among the \(18-45\) age group which representing a significant loss of the productive workforce. India accounts for almost 11% of global road accident deaths despite having only 1% of the world’s vehicles.
Continuous data collection and analysis help to identify accident-prone zones, black spots across highways and urban roads. Poor road conditions, lack of signage and faulty design are common contributors to these high-risk areas. The government has initiated steps such as iRAD to monitor and reduce accidents. Speeding, drunk driving and non-compliance with helmet and seatbelt rules are among the leading human factors. Overloaded and poorly maintained vehicles contribute significantly to accident rates.
Urban traffic congestion in metros adds the chaos and increasing the risk of collisions. The rapid rise in vehicle ownership in two-wheelers needs for stronger safety regulations. The motor vehicles act 2019 introduced stricter penalties to improve driver discipline. Awareness campaigns such as sadak suraksha jeevan raksha aim to educate citizens on road safety. But enforcement is a challenge due to manpower shortages and inconsistent monitoring.
Advanced traffic systems with AI-based monitoring are implemented in smart cities. School and college-based road safety education programs are important to build long term awareness7. Regular vehicle fitness checks and driver training need to be standardised across states. Collaboration with NGOs and the private sector enhances outreach engagement. Salem8 proposed a multi-agent V2V communication framework to enhance vehicle dynamics and cooperative driving through intelligent information exchange among connected vehicles. Real-time data analysis using GPS, CCTV and mobile apps helps to generate quicker response and trend identification9. Thanasupsin et al.10 developed a nested logit model to analyse travel mode choice behaviour within university campuses by examining multiple transportation preferences and influencing factors. When system need decision support system it can utilise adaptive artificial intelligence learning models within decision support systems to improve intelligent regional management under dynamic and data-driven environments11. Fadwa12 developed an integrated framework for multi-level production defect detection by combining quality management tools with maintenance optimisation strategies to improve industrial performance. Also, Tiryaki and Oral13 developed an advanced traffic sign classification framework using spatial transformer networks integrated with convolutional neural networks to improve recognition accuracy in intelligent transportation systems.
Tamil Nadu and Gujarat shown a reduction in accident rates through focused action plans. Still rural areas face challenges due to poor infrastructure and delayed emergency services. Continuous analysis include social, geographical and behavioral factors unique to each region. Multi agency coordination among transport, police, health and urban development departments is vital. India needs to meet its road safety targets, ongoing analysis, public participation and political will are essential14.
In India the analysis of road accidents involves uncertainty due to imprecise, incomplete data related to human behavior, road conditions and enforcement levels. To handle this uncertainty this model provides the framework of T2FS which allows for better modeling of the ambiguity present in expert opinions and accident-related factors. By incorporating aggregation operators diverse expert judgments and criteria can combine to evaluate accident prone areas. It introduces a novel distance measure designed for T2PF environments which enhances the precision of evaluations between alternatives. This integrated approach enables robust decision-making in identifying high risk zones and developing road safety interventions. Fuzzy sets
The concept of FS introduced by Zadeh in 196515. It was a groundbreaking step toward mathematical modeling and imprecision in real-world decision-making. Classical logic treats information in a binary manner but real-world problems such as economic forecasting and road accident analysis often involve vague data. FS addressed this by allowing partial membership and offering a flexible framework to capture gradations of truth which laid the foundation for several powerful extensions of fuzzy theory.
T1FS allow each element to have a degree of membership ranging from 0 to 1. But the membership of T2FS16 itself is uncertain such as when evaluating traffic risks and fluctuating economic indicators become essential. These sets model fuzziness in the membership function itself and providing an added layer of uncertainty modeling. IVT2FS17 are widely used due to their computational simplicity and effectiveness in capturing uncertainty ranges in problems.
To improve the representational accuracy of FS researchers have designed various fuzzy number shapes such as triangular, trapezoidal, pentagonal and heptagonal fuzzy numbers. Among these TrFNs are commonly employed for modeling economic intervals and estimating accident-related data that lie within approximate boundaries. Recently, Turgay et al.18 provided an uncertainty-aware evaluation framework based on T-spherical hesitant fuzzy rough sets for intelligent assessment of Edge-Cloud architectures in smart manufacturing.
Further enhancing the flexibility of fuzzy logic IFS19 introduce three components for each element. They are a degree of membership, non-membership and hesitation. This structure enables a deeper representation of expert uncertainty, such as in assessing regional economic instability or determining accident-prone zones where expert opinions may diverge. Several important extensions have emerged from this model:
- 
                    BIFS20 allow simultaneous representation of positive and negative perceptions which is valuable when analyzing conflicting public opinions about transportation safety.
- 
                    BVFS integrate both positive and negative contexts into a unified framework which useful in modeling dual-sided decision parameters.
- 
                    IVIFS accommodates ranges for both membership and non-membership values which ideal for capturing variability in economic metrics.
- 
                    T2IFS enhance capabilities by introducing non-membership to intuitionistic functions which suitable in high uncertainty domains.
Another milestone in fuzzy logic is the development of PyFS21. It extends IFN by allowing the sum of squares of membership and non-membership degrees to be at most 1. This extends the modeling capacity for highly uncertain environments. In applications such as urban traffic control, accident severity classification and economic impact assessment PyFS provides greater flexibility. It representing conflicting, incomplete and hesitant information. The evolution of FS theory from T1FS to advanced models such as T2FS, IFS and PyFS offers a powerful toolbox for analyzing complex socio-economic phenomena.
Literature review on MCDM methods in fuzzy environment
In recent decades MCDM methods have gained prominence for solving complex problems involving conflicting criteria. To better handle real-world uncertainty researchers have integrated MCDM methods with FS theory which leading to more flexible models. This review explores the evolution and application of various fuzzy-based MCDM approaches and highlighting their strengths, limitations and domains of use. Table 1 explains the recent works that used MCDM in the field of road accidents and economic strategy. Recently, Altayf et al.22 developed an MCDM framework for the intelligent selection of photovoltaic-battery energy storage systems (PV-BESS) by jointly evaluating cost and reliability factors. Mustafa et al.23 developed a GIS-based multi-criteria evaluation framework to assess land suitability for wind power farm development in Iraq by integrating environmental, spatial and technical factors. Chaoui et al.24 integrated geospatial technologies with multi-criteria decision analysis to enhance sustainable and resilient urban planning through comprehensive spatial and strategic evaluation. Qiu et al.25 developed a decision-making model for prioritising low-carbon policies by evaluating climate mitigation strategies under multiple sustainability criteria.
Motivation
Road traffic accidents in India have a severe public health concern and demanding immediate evaluation systems. Due to the inherent vagueness in expert assessments of accident-related factors traditional models having uncertainty. To address this issue this study proposes a novel decision-making framework based on T2PFS combined with advanced aggregation operators and a customized distance measure.
- 
                    This study motivated by the increasing level of road accidents in India. This critical issue demands investigation and an innovative assessment framework.
- 
                    Traditional statistical models are insufficient for handling the ambiguity, vagueness and subjectivity associated with real-world data. Hence it is important to explore an advanced fuzzy model to capture the imprecise nature of expert evaluations.
- 
                    Most existing models fail to consider the degree of hesitation in decision making. This motivation addresses the gap to utilise T2PFS which provides a richer structure for managing uncertainty, neutrality and disagreement in expert opinions.
- 
                    Road accident analysis involves multiple factors such as vehicle, infrastructure and environment. It makes traffic accident prioritisation as an ideal domain for applying MCDM methods. This motivated to structure the factors into a strong decision making framework.
- 
                    A motivation from the research opportunity is to develop novel aggregation operators and an innovative distance measure with the T2PFNs. It could enhance the precision of the final rankings.
- 
                    Literature survey revealed a scarcity of integrated studies that combine T2FL, PFS, advanced operators and a derived distance measures for road accident assessment. This gap motivated to contribute a unique and comprehensive model.
- 
                    Beyond academic interest this work strongly driven by the potential social impact. This research can assist policymakers and transportation authorities in prioritising road safety interventions.
The proposed fuzzy MCDM approach provides a proper evaluation of road accident risk factors under uncertainty. By incorporating T2PF modeling with a tailored distance measure this study offers a valuable insights for policy design and accident prevention strategies. This research opens new directions for applying advanced fuzzy models in other complex and uncertainty domains of public decision making.
Contribution
Road accidents is a pressing concern in India with increasing complex factors across regions. To address the challenge of uncertainty in evaluating accident risks this study adopt a T2PF framework. This study applies various fuzzy aggregation operators and a novel distance measure to assess 53 cities using 35 critical accident-related criteria.
- 
                    This study analyses road accident severity across 53 major cities which covering all states and union territories of India. It ensuring nationwide representation and applicability.
- 
                    A total of 35 critical criteria that including driver behavior, road infrastructure, vehicle conditions and environmental factors. They were identified and used to assess accident intensity in each city.
- 
                    The study introduces a novel decision-making framework which utilizing T2PFS along with various aggregation operators and a customized distance measure. It is effectively handling uncertainty, hesitation and contradiction in expert judgments.
- 
                    Using the proposed fuzzy MCDM model cities were ranked based on the severity and contributing factors of road accident. It helps to identify locations with the highest accident risk.
- 
                    Sensitivity analysis conducted to verify the stability of the city rankings under different weighting scenarios and operator choices.
- 
                    The findings were validated through appropriate statistical techniques which strengthening the credibility and real-world relevance of the proposed model.
The proposed model identifies the cities with high accident severity by capturing uncertainty in expert judgments. This study provides valuable insights for policymakers in prioritising strategies of road safety in India.

This article is organised into five sections. “Preliminaries” introduces the preliminary concepts including the mathematical foundation of T2PFNs and the proposed aggregation operators such as arithmetic, geometric, Hamy mean, Einstein weighted and Aczel-Alsina. “Case study: multi-criteria evaluation of road accidentseverity across cities” presents the real world case study involving road accident data from 53 Indian cities with the detailed algorithm designed to evaluate the cities using MCDM methods. “Results and validation” offers a discussion covering the results obtained from TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS and COPRAS with a sensitivity analysis. This section highlights the strengths, comparative advantages and limitations of the proposed framework. “Sensitivity analysis” focuses on the validation of the results which proving the consistency of rankings, implications for urban safety planning and the effectiveness of the proposed method under varying decision parameters. Finally “Conclusion” concludes the study by summarising the key findings, confirming the robustness of the model and suggesting directions for future research in decision-making under uncertainty. Proposed methodology
The proposed approach uses fuzzy aggregation, distance measures, and hybrid MCDM techniques to normalise data, evaluate alternatives, compute utility and significance scores, and then rank alternatives using integrated TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS, COPRAS and aggregation-based decision mechanisms as shown in Fig. 1.
Case study: multi-criteria evaluation of road accident severity across cities
To identify the city with the highest road accident rates specific evaluation criteria are essential. These 35 criteria provide a structured framework for comparing accident related factors across multiple cities. By analysing aspects such as accident frequency, severity and traffic conditions this work can gain a comprehensive understanding of accident trends.
- 
                  Speeding is one of the leading reasons to road accidents. It reduces the driver’s ability to react to sudden obstacles in traffic conditions. Higher speeds increase the crash and the severity of the resulting injuries36. It diminishes the effectiveness of safety measures such as seatbelts and airbags. It is making dangerous collisions.
- 
                  Drunk driving is a major cause of road accidents. It slows reaction time and reduces coordination. Drivers under this influence take risky actions, misjudge distances and fail to respond to traffic signals and hazards37. This reckless behavior increases the chances of collisions and resulting in severe injuries and fatalities.
- 
                  Mobile phone usage: using mobile phone while driving is a dangerous distraction that diverts the driver’s attention from the road. It reduces awareness and increases the missing traffic signals and obstacles38. Texting, calling and browsing in a mobile phone while driving elevates the risk of accidents.
- 
                  Violating traffic rules: ignoring signals and overtaking creates situations that increase the risk of accidents. These violations disrupt the flow of traffic and often lead to collisions39. Inconsistency in rules reflects poor traffic discipline and is a major contributor to road accidents.
- 
                  Driver fatigue: it affects a concentration of driver, reaction time and decision making ability. Tired drivers miss signals and fall asleep at the wheel. These are leading to serious accidents. Long hours of driving without rest are a common cause of fatigue related road incidents40.

Results and validation
The ranking of 53 Indian cities based on road accident data was performed using five well-established MCDM methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS and COPRAS. Each method produced an individual ranking list based on distinct criteria-weighted algorithms. Among all cities Chennai consistently showed lower severity values and received top positions across most methods. Specifically Chennai ranked 1st in TOPSIS, 3rd in VIKOR, 2nd in WASPAS, 2nd in CODAS and 1st in COPRAS. These consistent top ranks led Chennai to achieve the 1st place in the FIR64,65 and66 which confirming its outstanding road safety performance. Amritsar performed exceptionally well and securing ranks such as 3rd in TOPSIS and 1st in VIKOR and CODAS which reflects strong consistency in the results across diverse methods. Coimbatore and Chandigarh also maintained top 10 positions in most methods which demonstrating relatively safe traffic conditions and governance. Cities such as Kanpur, Lucknow and Ahmedabad consistently appeared in the bottom tier across all methods. For example Kanpur ranked 53rd in TOPSIS and 50th in VIKOR while Lucknow and Ahmedabad remained in the bottom 10 for all five methods. The rankings indicate road accident risks and the need of safety interventions.
Mid ranked cities such as Hyderabad, Pune and Rajkot showing the variations which reflecting their borderline performance and scope for improvement. To ensure the reliability of results the FIR calculated using an average rank aggregation across five methods. The FIR served as a comprehensive benchmark which is a minimising method in a specific bias and improving decision consistency. Cities with high ranks across methods maintained their position in the FIR which validating the robustness of the evaluation. The comparison revealed that top ranked cities in FIR such as Chennai, Amritsar and Coimbatore had lower sensitivity scores. It further validated the true values of their ranking. The cities with high FIR values corresponding to high sensitivity measures. This strong alignment between results and FIR ranking supports the validity of the applied MCDM models. The results identified high risk zones for policy focus and demonstrated the effectiveness of the multi-method approach in decision-making under uncertainty. Overall the rankings were found to be consistent, interpretable and statistically valid. It is strengthening their application in real-world traffic safety management.
Discussion
The FIR system provides an evaluation by integrating the outcomes of five MCDM methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS and COPRAS. This approach mitigates the inconsistencies among individual methods and yields a final ranking that captures the overall performance of each city. According to the FIR results Chennai stands out with the 1st rank and maintaining exceptional scores across all five methods. It is making that as the best performing city. Delhi follows closely in 2nd position which consistently placed in the top 10 by each method. Indore ranked 3rd which shows uniform excellence being ranked 1st by WASPAS and 2nd by TOPSIS and CODAS. Bengaluru secures the 4th FIR rank and indicating strong infrastructural service based efficiency. Dhanbad and Thrissur ranked 4th and 5th respectively. It is maintaining high positions across all models emphasising their consistent quality. Mumbai at 7th place performs steadily with all method based rankings placing it within the top 10.
On the other end of the spectrum Lucknow is the lowest-ranked city with an FIR of 53 consistently placed last by every method. Ghaziabad and Kanpur with FIRs of 52 and 50 also exhibit poor performance across all criteria suggesting systemic issues in their evaluated parameters. Coimbatore holds the 48th FIR rank matching low ranks across TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS and CODAS. Madurai and Nagpur follow with FIRs of 47 and 46 respectively and confirming the underwhelming evaluations by all individual methods. Amritsar though ranked 1st in VIKOR has a final FIR of 7 as it ranked lower in other methods such as COPRAS (6) and WASPAS (5) which shows how FIR effectively balances extremes. Kannur, Kozhikode and Ranchi with FIRs of 15, 14 and 15 respectively demonstrate variability in rankings but end up in the upper middle segment due to the fuzzy inference process averaging their performance. Jaipur, Jabalpur and Patna fall in the mid FIR range of 21 to 32 reflecting average performance across the board.
Tiruchirappalli and Durg Bhilainagar receiving better individual rankings which placed \(43\textrm{rd}\) and \(42\textrm{nd}\) respectively in FIR due to inconsistent scores from certain methods. Jodhpur given a very low rank by COPRAS \((53\textrm{rd})\) achieves a \(32\textrm{nd}\) FIR due to stable rankings in the other methods showing how FIR neutralizes the effect of outliers. Vijayawada and Vishakhapatnam both holding a \(42\textrm{nd}\) and \(44\textrm{th}\) FIR reflect steady low-to-moderate ranks across all methods. In the middle ranks Rajkot \((30\textrm{th})\), Raipur \((29\textrm{th})\) and Surat \((35\textrm{th})\) show moderate consistency without strong performance spikes. Kolkata despite being a major metropolitan city ranks 49th in FIR due to its consistently low placement across methods indicating performance concerns. Meanwhile Thrissur \((5\textrm{th})\) and Nasik \((9\textrm{th})\) shows how smaller cities can perform when evaluated on core efficiency metrics.
Results of the FIR ranking system provides a balanced insight into the performance of 53 Indian cities. It helps identify top cities for potential investment such as Chennai, Delhi and Indore. It is highlighting the areas in need of focused development efforts such as Lucknow, Ghaziabad and Kanpur. FIR offers a fair aggregated view by reconciling the strengths and weaknesses shown in each method. It ensures that no single evaluation criterion unfairly biases the final outcome. This makes FIR an essential tool in multi criteria city assessments and strategic planning. Figures 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 shows the variations in the rankings of MCDM methods.

Sensitivity analysis
Sensitivity analysis conducted to examine the variation in the rankings by changing the parameter q which influences the normalised values associated with road accidents across 53 Indian cities. The parameter q ranges from 2 to 500 and is used to observe the robustness of the decision-making outcomes under different sensitivity levels. Each city evaluated using normalised values for multiple q levels which allowing a comparative view of cities respond to changing conditions. It observed that an increase in q values gradually rise across all cities which indicating a consistent progression. This behavior confirms that the model produces proportional changes in sensitivity levels. Kanpur, Lucknow and Prayagraj consistently showed the higher sensitivity values in the entire range which suggesting exposure to road accident risks. Cities such as Chennai, Delhi and Amritsar exhibited lower values that showing less sensitivity to the parameter changes. Aurangabad, Faridabad and Jodhpur exhibited identical trends which suggesting similarities in their road safety profiles.
These overlapping trends are useful for regional policy formulation. Raipur, Ahmedabad and Madurai displayed sharper increases in values that indicating higher sensitivity and potential vulnerability. The analysis reveal sudden spikes in values which reinforces the reliability of the evaluation model. The data shows the variation which demonstrating the model is free from distortions. The consistency in value increments in q levels affirms that the decision framework same in different scenarios. Cities maintaining their relative positioning in most cases which supporting the ranking stability. Cities with higher initial values are high when q value increases thereby validating the robustness of the applied method. Clusters of cities with similar patterns can be used for zonal interventions and road safety policies. No substantial deviations were found during the sensitivity changing. This suggests that the weightings computations are well calibrated. Uniform behavior across cities indicate that no input criterion dominates the outcome unfairly. Finally, this analysis confirms the credibility of the decision making method and ensuring dependable policy insights under parameter fluctuations. Hence, the results of the model are interpretable to changes in sensitivity settings.
The results reveal that cities with high rankings remain unaffected by parameter shifts. Figure 9 confirms the reliability of the criteria and the effectiveness of the decision-making models. Therefore the sensitivity analysis validates the robustness of the findings.

Conclusion
This study analysed road accident severity across 53 major cities in India using a comprehensive MCDM framework based on 35 critical evaluation criteria capturing road safety, infrastructure, accident frequency and emergency response dimensions. To ensure robustness, five prominent MCDM methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS, and COPRAS were integrated with five distinct aggregation operators including arithmetic, geometric, Einstein, Aczel-Alsina and harmonic means. A major theoretical contribution of this work is the development and formal proof of a novel distance measure theorem under the T2PF environment enhancing decision precision, uncertainty modelling and comparative evaluation capability. The proposed framework generated city-wise rankings and integrated them into a FIR enabling balanced and comprehensive assessment across all methods. According to the FIR results, Chennai emerged as the best-performing city by securing the \(1^{st}\) rank with exceptional consistency across all five methods, indicating superior performance in road safety, infrastructure, and emergency response. Delhi and Indore followed in \(2^{nd}\) and \(3^{rd}\) positions respectively while Bengaluru, Dhanbad, Thrissur, Mumbai and Nasik also demonstrated strong and stable safety efficiency. These top-performing cities can serve as benchmark models for transportation planning and policy design.
Finally, this study provides mathematically rigorous T2PF decision-making framework. It delivers actionable policy guidance for city-specific accident prevention and transportation reform. By integrating multiple MCDM methods, advanced aggregation operators, entropy and the proposed novel distance measure the framework improves interpretability, reliability, and practical applicability for real-world road safety governance, enabling authorities to strategically identify benchmark cities, prioritise critical risk zones and implement targeted interventions for safer urban transportation systems.

MADURAI: Five members of a family were killed after the car they were travelling in collided with several vehicles and flipped over multiple times on the Thumbaipatti highway near Melur in Madurai early on Monday. Four others sustained injuries in the collision and are undergoing treatment at government hospitals.
The deceased were identified as K Sriram (32), his wife Ranchana (27), their one-and-a-half-year-old daughter Kiruthika, Sriram’s brother K Balaji (28) and their mother K Rajamery (50), all hailing from Chennai.
Sriram’s father, V Kanagaraj (55), who was also in the car, two bike riders, R Murugan (40) and C Murugan (55) of Sivaganga, and the driver of another car, J Prakash (40) from Madurai, sustained injuries.
Police said the incident occurred around 6.30am when Sriram and his family were on their way to attend a family function in Thoothukudi. Sriram, who was at the wheel, lost control of the car and hit a two-wheeler, driven by R Murugan, from behind.
To avoid further collision, he diverted the car to the right, but crossed over the median and hit another car — driven by Prakash — coming from the opposite direction.
Car driver may have dozed off at the wheel
The car rolled over multiple times before coming to a stop. While five occupants of the car died on the spot, the sixth occupant, Kanagaraj, survived with multiple injuries. He is currently undergoing treatment at Government Rajaji Hospital in Madurai.
Both the bike occupants and Prakash were admitted to the Government Hospital in Melur. Police suspect that Sriram may have dozed off at the wheel, leading to the accident. On receiving information, the Melur police along with fire and rescue services personnel extricated the bodies and sent them for postmortem examination. District Collector Nishanth Krishna inspected the spot.
summary: Five of Chennai family killed in Madurai crash The New Indian Express

Chennai: A Chennai motor accident claims tribunal has awarded ₹1.04 crore as compensation to the family of a woman dentist who was killed in a road accident in Neelathanallur, near Thanjavur in 2022.
As the dentist travelled in a goods carrier (Tata Ace), the tribunal granted the award after deducting 10% towards contributory negligence on part of the dentist. “The tribunal holds that the deceased has also contributed to some extent to her death in the unfortunate accident occurred and the extent of contribution is calculated as 10%,” A B Naseer Ali, judge of the tribunal said, and passed the award on a petition moved by the deceased Imayavalli’s husband U Radhakrishnan, minor son R I Hemdev Dharshan, her father M Selvam, and mother S G Jothi seeking ₹45 lakh as relief for the death caused to the deceased in the road accident.
Representing the petitioners, advocate A S Bilal submitted that on Aug 15, 2022, Radhakrishnan was driving a goods carrier at around 2.00pm in which Imayavalli and others were seated in the rear side. While they were proceeding near Asoor Kulam, Neelathanallur, another goods carrier driven by B Rajesh coming from the opposite direction, driven in a rash and negligent manner collided against their vehicle. Imayavalli died on the spot while others sustained injuries.
Opposing the plea, the insurer of Rajesh’s vehicle Magma HDI General Insurance Co Ltd contended that there was a delay of 182 days in filing the petition. It further argued that the deceased being a dentist should not have traveled in the rear portion of a goods vehicle, which is permitted only for carrying goods. “If she had averted traveling there, she would not have died and so, reasonable contributory negligence should be added to the accident,” the insurer said.
Recording the submissions, the tribunal directed payment of ₹2.32 lakh each to the parents of the deceased and ₹50 lakh each to her husband and son. The share of the son was directed to be deposited in a nationalised bank until he becomes a major.
summary: Tribunal orders ₹1Cr to family of dentist killed in road accident near Thanjavur in 2022 The Times of India
title: Tribunal orders ₹1Cr to family of dentist killed in road accident near Thanjavur in 2022 - The Times of India

A 26-year-old man, identified as Iraiyanbu, was killed in a road accident after the two-wheeler he was riding collided with a car belonging to Tamil Nadu minister Jagadeeswari in Kattankulathur near Chennai.
Jagadeeshwari is the Minister for Social Welfare and Women Empowerment.
According to reports, the minister’s vehicle was heading towards Chennai when the accident occurred.
Iraiyanbu, who was riding the two-wheeler, sustained severe injuries in the collision and died at the scene.
The car driver has been arrested.
Senior police sources said the minister was not in the car at the time of the accident. The personal vehicle was travelling along with the minister’s convoy, which was heading towards Chennai as Jagadeeswari was scheduled to attend the Legislative Assembly.
The car was registered in the minister’s name. Police arrested its 28-year-old driver, Chinna Agni, a resident of Madurai.
The Maraimalai Nagar Traffic Investigation Wing police seized the car and registered a case against Agni under Sections 281 (rash and negligent driving) and 106(1) (causing death by negligence) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Further investigation is under way.

MADURAI: Five members of a family, including a one-and-a-half-year-old girl, from Chennai were killed and four injured in a road accident on the Madurai–Tiruchy highway near Melur early on Tuesday.
Rajakumari (51), her sons, Balaji (31) and Sriram (27), Sriram's wife Ranjana, and their one-and-a-half-year-old daughter Praneeka Sri died on the spot. Police and Fire and Rescue Services personnel rescued Rajakumari’s husband Kanagaraj (55) from the wreckage.
He sustained grievous injuries and was rushed to the Government Rajaji Hospital.
The family was travelling to Kovilpatti in Thoothukudi after Balaji's wife, Aishwarya, gave birth to a baby in Kovilpatti. Balaji had travelled separately by bus and joined his family near Villupuram to travel together.
When the car driven by Sriram reached near the Thumbaipatti bridge, it grazed a motorcycle carrying two men. It then hit the median, crossed into the opposite carriageway, overturned and rolled several times. Worsening the accident, another car travelling from Madurai towards Tiruchy collided with the vehicle.
Prakash of Madurai, who was travelling in the other car, and the two motorcyclists, Murugan (55) and Murugan (40) of SV Mangalam near Singampunari, sustained injuries. They were admitted to the Melur Government Hospital for treatment.
After a prolonged rescue operation, the bodies of the five victims were retrieved from the mangled car and sent to the Melur Government Hospital for post-mortem examination.
Madurai Collector M Nishanth Krishna and Superintendent of Police BK Arvind Devanathan inspected the accident site and later visited the hospital to console the injured and their relatives.
Traffic on the four-lane highway was diverted through the service road for several hours following the accident.

 Four labourers, including three women, were killed and eight others injured after a mini van carrying woodcutters crashed into a tractor loaded with cashew firewood near Panruti in Cuddalore district in the early hours of Sunday.
The victims were identified as R Rani (60), R Ravi (58), K Gandhimathi (55) and S Sathya (32).
Police said the accident occurred around 4.30 am on National Highway 36 at Panikankuppam near Panruti. The mini van, carrying 11 daily wage labourers from Ayipettai and Venkatampettai to a wood-cutting site, was attempting to overtake a tractor transporting cashew firewood to Panruti when it rammed into the vehicle from behind.
The impact caused the stacked firewood logs on the tractor to topple onto the van, trapping the occupants inside.
Local residents rushed to the spot and helped rescue the victims from beneath the logs. The injured were taken to Panruti govt hospital in 108 ambulances. Rani and Ravi died on the way to the hospital, while Gandhimathi and Sathya later succumbed to their injuries at the Cuddalore govt hospital.
Eight others sustained serious injuries and are undergoing treatment at the Cuddalore govt hospital.
The accident disrupted traffic on the highway for some time before police cleared the vehicles and restored normal movement.
Kadampuliyur police have registered a case and detained the tractor driver for inquiry. Further investigations are under way to ascertain the circumstances that led to the crash.

Six persons including five passengers of two buses were killed after a Marthandam-bound omni bus collided with a TNSTC bus that was proceeding towards Tiruchi, near Karungalakudi on Madurai-Tiruchi highway in Madurai district in the early hours of Monday (July 13, 2026).
Forty passengers and crew members of both the buses were injured in the accident. The injured were rushed to Government Hospital in Melur, Government Rajaji Hospital (GRH) and a private hospital in Madurai.
The police said the driver of the omni bus lost control of the speeding vehicle and it suddenly swerved towards the right while it was proceeding at Vanjinagaram near Karungalakudi around 3.30 a.m.
The bus fell over the median and rammed against the TNSTC bus that was coming on the opposite lane. In the impact of the collision, the TNSTC bus turned turtle.
Within a few seconds, the omni bus turned towards the left and again jumped the median, the Superintendent of Police, Madurai district, N. Devanathan said. The omni bus came to a halt only after hitting the concrete bus shelter on the left side of the four-way highway.
Three passengers of the TNSTC bus, P. Anantharaj (46) of Tiruchi, K. Mohammed Yasin (60) of Tiruvarur and G. Surya (29) of Tiruchi, were killed on the spot. Two others travelling in the omni bus, J. Siriyapushpam (56) of Tirunelveli and J. Abraham, crew of the bus, from Thisayanvilai in Tirunelveli district, were also killed.
Senior police officers and firemen rushed to the spot and took up rescue operation.
C. Perumal (70) of Vanjinagaram, who was sleeping in the bus shelter sustained head injury. He was admitted to the GRH where he succumbed to injuries later.
While others were treated as outpatients at different hospitals, a total of 19 victims were admitted to the hospitals. A girl from Tiruchi suffered fracture on her shoulder, and many of them have suffered head injuries.
Madurai district police are investigating.
Madurai District Collector Nishanth Krishna, MP Su Venkatesan and others visited the hospital and inquired with the doctors about the treatment being given to the injured persons.
CM announces solatium
Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay has announced an ex gratia of ₹3 lakh each to the families of those killed in the road accident.

The Madras High Court has upheld a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal award of ₹2.92 crore to the family of an ISRO scientist who died after his motorcycle collided with a parked TATA Ace vehicle on Chennai's Outer Ring Road. Rejecting the insurer's plea that the deceased was partly responsible for the accident, the court held that the dangerous parking of the goods vehicle was the sole cause of the fatal crash.
Background of the Case
The case arose from an accident on December 31, 2019, when R.S. Pugazhenthi, a scientist at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, was riding his motorcycle on the Minjur–Vandalur Outer Ring Road. His motorcycle struck the rear of a TATA Ace vehicle that had been parked on the left side of the road near the entry to an elevated stretch without adequate warning. He suffered fatal injuries at the scene.
His wife, minor son and mother approached the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Thiruvallur, seeking compensation. The Tribunal found the driver of the TATA Ace negligent and awarded compensation of ₹2,92,69,944 with interest. Tata AIG General Insurance challenged that finding before the High Court.
Court's Observations
A Division Bench comprising Justice C.V. Karthikeyan and Justice K. Rajasekar examined the evidence of the eyewitness, the driver of the parked vehicle, the FIR, photographs and the Motor Vehicle Inspection Report.
The court noted that the TATA Ace had been parked on the lane generally used by two-wheelers at the entry to an elevated section of the Outer Ring Road, where visibility was limited because of the slope.
The bench observed,
"The parking of TATA Ace vehicle was the root cause for the accident." 
It further held that although the deceased may have been travelling at a high speed, that alone could not amount to negligence because the Outer Ring Road was specifically designed for fast-moving traffic.
Rejecting the insurer's argument of contributory negligence, the court said,
"Fixing up of contributory negligence on the deceased would not be proper," adding that the vehicle had been parked at a crucial point on the road, triggering the collision.
The judges also took note of the police investigation, which resulted in a charge sheet against the driver of the parked vehicle, observing that there was no material to rebut those proceedings.
Decision
Finding no error in the Tribunal's conclusion on negligence, the High Court confirmed that the accident occurred solely because of the negligent parking of the TATA Ace vehicle. Since the insurer had not challenged the quantum of compensation, the court also upheld the compensation awarded by the Tribunal.
Accordingly, the Civil Miscellaneous Appeal filed by Tata AIG General Insurance Company Ltd. was dismissed, and the Tribunal's award remained unchanged.
Case Details
Case Title: Tata AIG General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. P. Ammu & Others

The Greater Chennai City Traffic Police (GCTP) has said that fatalities due to road accidents declined by over 10% in 2025 compared to 2024, as of December 23.
While 534 fatalities were recorded up to December 15 last year, the number reduced to 479 during the corresponding period in 2025. In addition, grievous hurt cases saw a substantial 64% drop, falling from 2,093 cases last year to 721 this year.
Road accidents rise
However, the total number of road accidents increased to 3,981 this year from 3,753 last year, marking a rise of 6.07%. Police officials said efforts are under way to bring accident numbers down and maintain them at the previous year’s level.
Greater Chennai City Police Commissioner A. Arun said fatalities had been reduced by over 10% compared to last year, and grievous hurt cases had dropped significantly. He added that the GCTP would continue its efforts to reduce accidents and ensure road safety as a top priority.
According to statistics provided by the GCTP, during the corresponding period last year up to December 22, 2024, 3,753 accidents were recorded, resulting in 534 fatalities. Grievous injury cases stood at 2,140, simple injury cases at 941, and 138 accidents were reported with no injuries.
As of December 22, this year, a total of 3,981 accidents were reported, resulting in 479 fatalities. Of these, 754 cases involved grievous injuries, 2,630 involved simple injuries, and 118 were reported as no-injury accidents, where vehicles were damaged but occupants were unharmed.
This year, most motor accidents occurred during peak hours between 9 a.m. and 12 noon, with 711 incidents reported during this period. This was followed by 615 accidents between 3 p.m. and 6 p.m., and 602 accidents between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.
Fewer accidents on weekends
Accidents were comparatively fewer on Saturdays and Sundays than on weekdays, owing to strict enforcement measures. Statistics show 588 accidents on Saturdays and 578 on Sundays.
Two-wheeler accidents accounted for a major share of road mishaps, with 1,573 such accidents reported and 2,076 persons either injured or killed. In addition, 878 cars, 378 autos, 176 buses, 280 lorries, and 275 vans were involved in road accidents.
Additional Commissioner of Police (Traffic) G. Karthikeyan said the GCTP has undertaken various steps and remedial measures to reduce road accidents and enhance road safety across the city through increased enforcement, patrolling, and awareness activities. He added that the GCTP creates impactful awareness among road users by urging the public to maintain road discipline, follow safety guidelines, use protective gear, and educate themselves on road safety.
In coordination with experts, the GCTP has facilitated several training programmes for police personnel on technological approaches to accident reduction, along with workshops and safety education programmes for schoolchildren, bus drivers, and delivery agents. In addition to awareness campaigns, the GCTP has strengthened its enforcement strategy by booking more cases for over speeding, drunken driving, and riding without helmets through manual checks and technological initiatives such as ANPR cameras, 2D speed radar systems, and vehicle interceptor systems across Chennai city.
Joint Commissioner of Police (South) P. Vijayakumar said, “We are constantly monitoring accidents through our real-time monitoring system. If the accident rate rises in any particular area, the concerned officer will be asked to explain the cause or any lacunae in enforcement. We are analysing whether accidents are due to human error or infrastructure issues. Furthermore, the GCTP is continuously taking steps to improve road conditions, signage, and lighting at identified hotspots and accident-prone zones. These collective efforts have led to a significant reduction in road accident fatalities compared to last year in Chennai city.”

IIT Madras' Centre of Excellence for Road Safety hosts 'Zero Accident Day' Campaign in partnership with Greater Chennai Traffic Police
- 9th Aug 2024
- 
            Press Release
The road network in India has grown at a rate of 59% in the past nine years and stands as second in the world with the largest road network of 66.71 lakh km as of 2023. Every year, the country loses an average of 1,50,000 people to road accidents, of whom 25% of people are under 25 years old and 89% of people are under 60 years old.
These are the productive working population of India, leading to a tremendous socio-economic loss for families, society and the Nation. 
The Centre of Excellence for Road Safety, IIT Madras, is working with the Greater Chennai Traffic Police (GCTP) on multiple capacity and capability improvement programs. As many as 69 investigating officers (IOs) have been upskilled in performing scientific crash investigations to identify the root causes of the crashes. A total of 40 children and 80 schoolteachers and parents were introduced to gamified activity-based learning of road safety to improve their knowledge and cognition on being an informed road user. 
The awareness campaign for 'Zero Accident Day '(ZAD) was inaugurated at the Metropolitan Transport Corporation (MTC) Depot by Thiru R Sudhakar, IPS, Additional Commissioner of Police (Traffic), GCTP, in the presence of Dr Alby John Varghese, IAS, Managing Director, Metropolitan Transport Corporation (MTC), Professor Venkatesh Balasubramanian, Head, CoERS, IIT Madras, Thiru Bandi Gangadhar, IPS, Deputy Commissioner of Police, (Traffic) South, Thiru P Kumar, Deputy Commissioner of Police, (Traffic) North, and Thiru V Baskaran, Deputy Commissioner of Police, (Traffic) East. 
CoERS organized capacity building workshops at IIT Madras to drive activity-based learning (ABL) on road safety rules, signages and etiquette for Metropolitan Transport Corporation (MTC) bus drivers, school children, teachers and traffic wardens. In Addition, GCTP has engineered several initiatives at community level, such as engaging the vibrant youth as stakeholders, by means of a reel making competition, and several flashmobs are part of the campaign.  
Programmes are also underway to engage other sections of society including sensitising e-commerce platforms and their staff, IT firms, and engagements with hospitals, auto-rickshaw drivers, residential associations and slums. Activities to incentivise compliance with road rules such as traffic signal, seatbelts, helmets and stop line programmes are also a part of Zero Accident Day campaign.  
Speaking on the occasion, Prof. V. Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras, said, "At IIT Madras, we believe in providing solutions to everyday problems that plague our society. Road safety is matter of vital importance, given its long-term implications on the socio-economic status of accident victims. Bringing down road crash fatalities is a crucial step in increasing the standard of living in our Country. We are hopeful that this initiative by CoERS, IIT Madras and GCTP will yield positive results by enabling the required mind set change among the general public. We need more such awareness programmes to sensitise road users on safe driving practices."
Addressing the inaugural programme, Thiru Alby John Varghese, IAS, Managing Director, Metropolitan Transport Corporation (Chennai) Limited, said, "Zero accident day is an innovative concept where we are creating awareness on different subjects on different days. MTC buses play a large role in the movement of vehicles in our city. Our bus drivers drive 100s of kilometres in a day and do it under stressful conditions. This training programme as part of the ZAD campaign with IIT Madras will help them better navigate the city's roads and make them both better drivers and role models for other drivers." 
The MTC Drivers were provided 'simulator-based training in safe driving concepts, hazard perception, and driving etiquette which will go a long way in improving their ability to drive safely. 
Emphasising the necessity of training future drivers, Thiru Sreenivasan Janakiraman, CSR Head, Ford Motor Private Limited, said, "To tap into India's demographic dividend, it's very important to take action today
to create responsible road users for the future. As an automotive company, we understand that road safety is critical and we are glad to be a part of this initiative to train young drivers and make our roads safer." 
Commending this IIT Madras initiative, Thiru R Sudhakar, IPS, Additional Commissioner of Police, Greater Chennai Traffic Police, said, "Every city across the world witnesses accidents. Our aim has always been to bring down road accidents and fatalities and make Chennai a zero-accident city, even if it is for one day. We're happy to partner with CoERS and IIT Madras to make this happen. Normally when someone says Zero, there is a negative image attached to it. We wanted to change this, and give zero a positive changeover. This ZAD campaign is for 20 days with different stakeholders with a unique theme for each day to create maximum awareness and impact." 
Elaborating on the programme, Prof. Venkatesh Balasubramanian, Head, CoERS and RBG Labs, Department of Engineering Design, IIT Madras, who is coordinating this initiative, said, "Road users need to be continuously refreshed on knowledge of road rules, proper driving etiquette, violations, and negligent driving behaviour that cause road safety hazards to people, infrastructure, and vehicles. Enforcement could provide interventions only to a limited extent to maintain the safety of all road users. This vision Zero Accidents in Chennai is within reach but can only become a reality if all of us undergo a behavioural and mindset change to educate ourselves to be responsible road users."
This entire month of the Zero Accident Day (ZAD) campaign by GCTP will be about road safety education and awareness for all road users in Chennai at all age levels. Several activities at the community level, schools, colleges, IT parks are planned in Chennai as an endeavour towards making Chennai roads safe.
The Centre of Excellence in Road Safety (CoERS) at IIT Madras is funded by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), Government of India, to perform evidence-based integrated approach to Road Safety. CoERS works on various aspects of human factors engineering, road engineering and vehicle engineering to bring about significant improvements in road safety globally. This CoERS also advices various stakeholders and Governments to bring about a data-driven systems approach to road safety.

Good Samaritans who rescue victims of serious road accidents and rush them to a hospital within the golden hour will now be rewarded with ₹5,000. They will also be eligible for a cash prize of ₹1 lakh which will be given to 10 such Samaritans in a year.
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways wrote to all States and Union Territories on Monday informing them of the new scheme, which comes into effect from October 15, 2021 till March 31, 2026.
Need to motivate general public
“It has been felt that there is a need to motivate the general public through cash awards and certificates to help the road accident victims in emergency situation and to boost their morale, and also to inspire and motivate others to save the lives of the victims,” according to the letter dated October 3, 2021.
The categories of accidents that will make one eligible for the award will include those that result in a major surgery or minimum three days of hospitalisation or brain and spinal cord injuries.
The ‘golden hour’ has been defined as ‘the time period lasting one hour following a traumatic injury during which there is the highest likelihood of preventing death by providing prompt medical care’.
The award will be ₹5,000 per victim saved and if more than one bystander is involved then the prize will be divided equally among them. Every cash award will be accompanied with a certificate of appreciation. An individual can be awarded a maximum of five times in a year.
Initial grant
The Centre will provide ₹5 lakh as initial grant to the Transport Departments for the scheme.
The guidelines also lay down the procedure to be followed for authenticating beneficiaries. The local police will take details from the doctor and provide an acknowledgment to the bystander who helped. A copy of this will then be sent by the police to an appraisal committee formed at the district level under the chairmanship of a district Magistrate, which will approve the proposals on a monthly basis.

New Delhi: Nearly a decade ago, Deepanshu was in Class 11 when a road accident in Laxmi Nagar left his father bedridden for two years.
That moment upended his family's life. It also gave him his life's mission. He went on to found the India Road Safety Council and later joined Crashfree India, a movement dedicated to safer roads.
His co-founder, Amar, experienced a similar wake-up call as an IIT student when some friends were seriously injured in a road crash. 
"More than the accident itself, what stayed with me was seeing my mother struggle," Deepanshu recalled. "Our lives were completely turned upside down. Financially, we were stretched thin. My brother had to start working early, and I had to figure out ways to support the family while in Class XI. We didn't know how the compensation process worked and felt helpless. That's when I realised just how many gaps exist in the system."
On Sunday, CrashFree India organised the NextMile: Road Safety Policy Ideathon at the India Habitat Centre. Ten finalist teams from across the country pitched ideas, guided by mentors, including IIT professors, legal experts and practitioners.
The discussions covered a wide array of topics. Some teams focused on protecting delivery riders who cater to quick-commerce deliveries. 
Others explored black-spot rectification. Crash data transparency, emergency response protocols, insurance and compensation, and speed management were also discussed.
The winners, Team Strategist, zeroed in on the safety of quick-commerce delivery agents. 
In Aug, a 40-year-old delivery executive died in a hit-and-run after his e-scooter was struck by a negligently driven SUV in Vasant Kunj (north).
With little formal training, long working hours and the constant pressure of deadlines, the workers are among the most vulnerable. 
Team Strategist proposed a city-wide driver permit system that would require road safety training and practical driving tests before riders begin work. This would raise the minimum competency level and enforce essentials like helmet use and functioning brakes.
Building on a 5S framework — safe speed, safe streets, safe spaces, safe system, safe road users — the team's suggestion went beyond licensing. It tackled speed and fatigue, which it categorised as a "silent killer." 
Their proposal included a digital platform that enforced rest breaks through "cooling-off" periods and designated rest zones — inspired by Chennai's rider rest pods. "The one in Chennai have AC. We can implement multiple grassroots-level pods," the team said.
The team also proposed a 1% levy on transactions for a city-level rider safety fund. It suggested integrating police accident data into a centralised platform to speed up black-spot rectification.
Another winning team, Safer Miles, addressed compensation delays. It pitched SurakshaSetu, a one-stop digital crash compensation platform powered by blockchain and smart contracts. Its solution tackled a chronic problem: the long delays in accessing accident compensation. It proposed linking FIRs, hospitals and insurers in real time, so that victims get quick financial relief. Automatic triggers would handle SMS claim tracking and hospital treatment linking.
Other ideas also sparked discussion, especially around black-spot rectification and data-driven safety. 
Spme of the solutions included a centralised platform for agencies and resident welfare associations, alerts for drivers in high-risk zones, maps of safest routes, citizen reporting on road flaws, and integrated monitoring systems with police for quick follow-up. 
Deepanshu said: "We will try to take the ideathon's inputs forward and present the ideas of the top three teams at the policy level. If approved, the pilot will begin in Delhi."

Chennai, Nov 24: In a devastating road accident, six passengers were killed and more than 20 others were injured when two buses collided head-on near Duraisamipuram, close to Kadayanaallur in Tenkasi district.
The incident occurred around 11 a.m. and immediately sent shockwaves through the region.
According to police sources, a private KSR bus was travelling towards Tenkasi when it reached Duraisamipuram junction. At the same time, another bus — operated by MR Gopalan Travels and heading from Kovilpatti to Tenkasi — was approaching from the opposite direction. In a split second, both vehicles rammed into each other with immense force, trapping several passengers inside.
Local residents, who rushed to the spot upon hearing the loud crash, joined police and fire-rescue teams in pulling out the injured.
The Tenkasi district administration, led by District Collector and District Superintendent of Police reached the site within minutes and is supervising rescue operations, which are still underway.
The injured have been admitted to Tenkasi Government Medical College Hospital, where several remain in critical condition. Officials fear that the death toll may rise.
Eyewitnesses described scenes of chaos, with shattered glass and twisted metal scattered across the road. Several passengers had to be extricated using hydraulic cutters, and emergency teams faced considerable difficulty due to the impact of the collision.
Monday‘s accident comes at a time when Tamil Nadu has witnessed multiple fatal mishaps in a short span, raising serious concerns about road safety and vehicle regulation.
Just days ago, four members of a family died in Tiruvannamalai district after their car collided with a lorry. In another incident in Coimbatore, two college students were killed when their motorcycle was hit by a speeding bus.
Last week, three persons lost their lives in Ramanathapuram after a private van overturned due to reckless driving. Data from the state transport department indicates that Tamil Nadu continues to rank among the states with the highest number of road fatalities in India.
Police officials say speeding, fatigue of long-distance drivers, and poor enforcement continue to be major factors.
As rescue teams continue their work at Duraisamipuram, authorities have ordered a detailed enquiry into the cause of the collision. The tragic accident has once again underscored the urgent need for stricter safety protocols and regular inspection of private buses operating on busy inter-district routes.
--IANS
summary: Tenkasi tragedy: Six dead, over 20 hurt in Tamil Nadu bus crash The Assam Tribune

Schools and Other Disasters
Since 2005, the NGO Pratham has been publishing ASERs (Annual Status of Education Reports); a nationwide survey of children’s ability to read simple text, and do basic arithmetic.
The cities surveyed include Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Bhopal, Chennai, Delhi, Jaipur, Jamshedpur, Kanpur, Kolkata, Lucknow, Mumbai, Patna, Pune, and Vijayawada.
Over 11,000 children below the age of 18 were killed in road crashes in 2019 in India, revealed the data provided by the Ministry of Roads Transport and Highways (MoRTH),
While the nation celebrates Children’s Day every year on 14 November, there are some starling facts revealed in a survey that how vulnerable are the children while travelling to their schools, colleges due to poor road planning and poor traffic behaviour.
Advertisement
According to the MoRTH, Indian roads reported over 30 deaths daily, with a 7.4% contribution to the total road crash deaths. Children face a high degree of risk while commuting to and from school due to poor road planning, limited enforcement and poor traffic behaviour
Recently, a national study by SaveLIFE Foundation highlighted the gaps in road safety for children. The study reviews the existing status of school transport together with bringing out the challenges and areas of improvement.
The study conducted after the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, analyses responses from 11,845 respondents, including 5,711 children (of classes 6-12) and 6,134 parents (with children in classes 1-12) across 14 cities in India with the intent of gathering insights across age-groups and geographies to inform how we can improve the road safety of children while they commute to school.
According to the NGO, some of the key findings include 47% of the surveyed respondents using school transport admitted to their school vehicles not being equipped with seat belts.
While 34% of the respondents using two-wheelers surveyed had not ensured their child that they were wearing a helmet while commuting via two-wheelers.
Besides, 30% of children witnessed a crash during their commute to school, while 6% of them were themselves involved in a road crash or a near-miss situation during their commute to and from school.
“This finding is significant given over 30 children lose their lives on India’s roads every day,” reveals the survey report.
Additionally, more than half of the parents surveyed stated that school authorities took no action on the safety concerns reported to the school authorities.
“These issues included overcrowding in school vehicles, congestion near the school, and over-speeding by drivers in the school zone,” stated the survey.
47% of the surveyed respondents whose child who cycled to school reported no cycling paths en route or even around the school. 30% of those whose children who walked to school reported missing footpaths around the school zone.
The study has proposed some programs to build awareness among parents to equip them to ensure that schools adhere to safety norms.
Commenting on the same, Piyush Tewari, Founder & CEO, SaveLIFE Foundation said, “As of date, over 25 states and Union Territories have announced the reopening of schools. While there is a vaccine for COVID, the vaccine for child deaths on our roads is really our collective action.”
He further said, “Our findings through this report have once again emphasised that the right to a safe commute to school is as important as the right to education itself. A comprehensive national and state school transport safety policy can ensure that.”

LONDON: An inquest into the deaths of eight Indians killed last month in one of the UK's worst road accidents was suspended on Tuesday pending police investigation, just hours after it was opened.
The inquest by Coroner Tom Osborne at the Crownhill Crematorium site on Dansteed Way in Milton Keynes, southern England, formally identified the victims as Indians based in the UK and some of their friends and members of their families who were in the UK as tourists.
Those who died in the collision have been formally named as Karthikeyan Pugalur Ramasubramanian, 33, and his wife, Lavanyalakshmi Seetharaman, 32, who were from the Alwarthirunagar area of Chennai; Panneerselvam Annamalai, 63, from the Nagar area of Chennai; Subramaniyan Arachelvan, 58, and his wife Tamilmani Arachelvan, 50, from the Saket area of Delhi; Vivek Baskaran, 26, from the Avaiyambalpuram area of Mayiladuthurai; Rishi Rajeev Kumar, 27, from Kerala and [British Indian] Cyriac Joseph, 52, who lived in Nottingham, a Thames Valley Police statement said today.
Chief Inspector Henry Parsons, from the force's Joint Operations Unit for Roads Policing, said his team is conducting a "substantial" police investigation into the crash after which the inquest into the deaths can be closed.
"We are continuing to support and update the families of those who died in the collision, as well as those who were injured and remain in hospital. Our thoughts remain with everyone involved at this time," he said.
Karthikeyan Ramasubramaniyam Pugalur, Rishi Rajeev Kumar, and Vivek Bhaskaran had been identified by Indian software company Wipro as its employees who were among those killed in the deadly accident on a highway in Buckinghamshire, southern England, when the mini bus they were travelling in got crushed between two large trucks.
Shravathi Ramasubramanian, the four-year-old daughter of Karthikeyan and Lavanyalakshmi who died in the accident, is being cared for by two of her relatives at Birmingham Children's hospital and her condition is said to be stable.
Three others hospitalised after the crash include Mano Ranjan Panneerselvam, another Wipro employee, at St John Radcliffe Hospital, his wife at Milton Keynes Hospital, and his aunt at Cardiff hospital.
They are in a stable condition and their condition is improving, said Jacob Ravibalan, chair of the World Tamil Organisation (UK) - a group that is providing support on the ground.
"After the coroner hands over the bodies to funeral directors, we are expecting that their reparation to India can take place by this weekend," he said.
Cyriac Joseph, the Kerala-born owner of Nottingham-based ABC Travels and driver of the minibus who was among those who lost their lives in the highway pile-up, is expected to be given his last rites in the UK.
The fatal collision took place on the M1 motorway near Newport Pagnell in the early hours of August 26 as the families from India were en-route from Nottingham to London to set off on a European holiday.
Two lorry drivers - Ryszard Masierak and David Wagstaff - have since been charged with causing death by dangerous driving and are set to appear in court later this month.
Masierak, who will appear at Aylesbury Crown Court on September 26, has also been charged with being almost twice the legal drink drive limit at the time of the crash.
Wagstaff will appear before Milton Keynes Magistrates' Court on September 11.
summary: Inquest into death of eight Indians in UK road crash suspended The Times of India

Man returning to Hosur after meeting in-laws, his friend die as car jumps divider, hits bus
Two men were charred to death in a horrific incident onHosur Road  in the early hours of Sunday.
The i20 that the two – Zabbiullah and Ismail – were travelling in hit the divider near Chandapura, jumped the median and crashed into an oncoming private bus. The car exploded into a ball of fire and the two passengers were charred beyond recognition.
The bus also caught fire and all the 20 passengers had a miraculous escape – they managed to get off the bus before the fire spread and gutted both the vehicles. The bus was headed to Bengaluru fromChennai .
“We are investigating the matter. As of now, it seems that the petrol tank of the vehicle got ruptured and fuel was leaking after the car got lodged under the bus. There must have been a spark which started the fire,” said TP Shivakumar, Superintendent, Bengaluru Police (Rural).
According to Surya city police, the mishap is expected to have occurred around 4.30 am. Zabbiullah (24) and Ismail (28) were heading towards Hosur in Tamil Nadu. Zabbiullah, a manager in a real estate firm in Hosur, had come to Bengaluru to meet his in-laws residing inMalleswaram . Ismail, employed as a driver in Tamil Nadu , had also accompanied Zabbiullah to Bengaluru.
“Zabbiullah was in the driver’s seat and Ismael was on the passenger side. The entire car was mangled and stuck underneath the interstate private bus plying forGreenline  travels. The car had first rammed into the median and had flipped over onto the path of the bus which rammed into it. We suspect that the car driver could have dozed off and lost control,” said Surya city police.
As soon as the fire broke out the bus passengers got off and emergency and fire personnel were alerted. However, the fire spread quickly and both the vehicles were gutted. Though both men were trapped inside the car, none of the passengers and police could approach the vehicle as it was completely engulfed in flames within a few seconds.
“We received a call at 5 am and one fire tender fromElectronics City  station reached the spot within 10 minutes and brought the fire under control,” said a fire service personnel.
Police said that the exact cause for the fire would be ascertained after forensic analysis. Surya city police also added that prima facie it looked like the bus driver was not at fault for the mishap. A case under section 304 (A) will be filed after initial round of probe. The bodies would be handed over to the relatives after autopsy.

CAIRO, Oct 15 (Reuters) Fourteen Egyptian military conscripts and a civilian driver were killed today when a minibus and a water tanker collided on a road in the Sinai peninsula, security sources said.
The sources said the accident happened when the vehicles crashed head-on on an intercity road in south Sinai as the soldiers were returning in the minibus to Sharm el-Sheikh at the end of the Eid el-Fitr Muslim holiday.
The accident came a day after at least six people, mostly children, died in a Nile river ferry accident in Minya province, south of Cairo.
Reckless driving, lax traffic rules and poor road conditions cause many road crashes in Egypt. A series of road and rail accidents in the past few years triggered a public outcry over the government's handling of road and transport safety.
